summary: This standards-track document specifies mapping between X.400 messaging, as defined by ITU-T recommendations, and Internet mail in RFC 822 and MIME. It lets gateways translate messages between the two systems.

plainLanguage.summary: MIXER defines how a mail gateway translates between X.400 and RFC 822/MIME systems. It maps addresses, message fields, and mail services, while documenting features that cannot cross the boundary.

questions: how does x.400 map to rfc 822
what is an x.400 or address
subtitle: A gateway specification for mapping messages and addresses between X.400 and Internet mail.

tldr.problem: X.400 and RFC 822/MIME mail use different address systems, message structures, and service features. A message crossing between them needs consistent translation, including when it passes several gateways.
tldr.mechanism: MIXER maps X.400 interpersonal messages and transfer information to RFC 822 messages and SMTP information. It defines address representations, global mapping tables, and mappings for headers and services.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2156 obsoletes RFCs 987, 1026, 1138, 1148, 1327, and 1495, and updates RFC 822. Body-part mapping is in companion RFC 2157.

today: RFC 2156 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1998. It obsoletes RFC 987, RFC 1026, RFC 1138, RFC 1148, RFC 1327, and RFC 1495, and updates RFC 822. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Mail Systems Need Consistent Translation
sections.content:
X.400 defines an interpersonal messaging system and a store-and-forward transfer system. Internet mail combines the RFC 822 header format with MIME body formats and commonly uses SMTP for transfer. Because communities using one system need to reach users on the other, multiple gateways may handle the same message.

RFC 2156, called MIXER, aims to make those gateways behave consistently, preserve information, and make mappings reversible where possible. It targets the global scenario, where two mail networks connect through multiple gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 and Internet mail represent addresses and messages differently. MIXER gives gateways common translation rules so messages can cross between the systems.

sections.title: What a Gateway Translates
sections.content:
An X.400 interpersonal message contains a heading and a body made of body parts. Its message transfer envelope contains an identifier, sender, and recipient list. An RFC 822 message has a header and content, while its underlying transfer service identifies recipients and an error-return address.

The parts do not map one-to-one. An RFC 822 message plus SMTP information becomes an X.400 interpersonal message; a delivery-status notification becomes an X.400 report. In the reverse direction, X.400 messages and notifications become RFC 822 messages, and reports become delivery-status notifications. Body-part mapping is specified separately in RFC 2157.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway translates both message content and transfer information. Some features map directly; others need special fields or cannot be represented on the other system.

sections.title: How Much of a Service Maps
sections.content:
MIXER classifies service support as supported, partially supported, or not supported. A fully supported service has matching meaning, no significant information loss, and any required action is carried out. Some RFC 822 headers map directly to X.400 heading fields.

Headers with no direct X.400 equivalent, including unknown and X-* fields, can be carried in a heading extension. X.400 features that RFC 822 cannot express may use newly defined RFC 822 headers. Security services such as content confidentiality and integrity are not mapped.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail features translate directly, some are carried as extra information, and some have no equivalent. The gateway rules identify which case applies.

sections.title: Mapping Mail Addresses
sections.content:
An X.400 OR Address is an ordered set of attributes such as country, administration domain, organization, organizational units, and a person's name. MIXER defines a text representation for these attributes inside an RFC 822 address. A simpler form is available for common personal names.

MIXER also defines a MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping (MCGAM), which connects a point in the Internet domain hierarchy with a point in the X.400 address hierarchy. These mappings can be distributed as tables, through DNS, or through X.500. When a normal mapping does not apply, an RFC-822 domain-defined attribute can preserve the Internet address for a return path.
sections.plainLanguage: The two systems arrange address parts differently. A global mapping connects matching parts of their hierarchies, and a special attribute can carry an Internet address that has no direct X.400 form.

sections.title: Mapping Headers and Reports
sections.content:
The detailed rules map RFC 822 headers to X.400 heading fields. For example, To becomes primary recipients, Cc becomes copy recipients, Reply-To becomes reply recipients, and Subject becomes the subject. Headers without a defined mapping may be preserved in an extension field.

In the reverse direction, the gateway creates an RFC 822 message from an X.400 message, report, or notification. It generates required fields such as Date and From when needed. Gateways count MIXER conversions; more than five in one direction is treated as a detected loop.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway applies field-by-field rules to translate headers and reports. It also counts repeated conversions so a message cannot circulate between systems indefinitely.

sections.title: Conforming Gateway Requirements
sections.content:
A conforming gateway must implement mandatory field formats, global address mappings, trace mappings, and the body-part rules in RFC 2157. It must identify the transfer protocols and X.400 versions it supports, and state how it accesses global address mappings. A subset that omits mandatory features is not conformant.

The specification does not provide access to every X.400 service and is not an X.400 user interface. It is designed to preserve existing Internet mail service while allowing selected X.400 features to cross the gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: A conforming gateway must state which protocols and X.400 versions it supports and implement the required mappings. MIXER does not expose every X.400 feature to Internet mail users.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo. Its service mapping discussion identifies X.400 confidentiality, integrity, message-sequence integrity, proof of delivery, and related security services as not supported across the gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not analyze security. It identifies several X.400 security services that do not map across to RFC 822 mail.
